summary: Teach the star life cycle (ages 9-11) as a story with one branch point decided by MASS: all stars are born in clouds of gas and dust (nebulae) that gravity pulls together until the core is hot and dense enough to fuse hydrogen into helium — which is what makes a star shine for millions to billions of years on the stable main sequence. When core hydrogen runs low the star swells and dies, and HOW it dies depends on mass: lower-mass Sun-like stars swell to a giant, puff off their outer layers and leave a cooling white dwarf, while very massive stars swell to a supergiant and end in a supernova. Two big ideas: the born→shine→die sequence powered by fusion, and mass deciding the ending (including the surprising twist that bigger stars live SHORTER lives). A mass-controlled interactive may be a particularly direct way for a learner to discover mass→fate; a labelled branching diagram, awe imagery, and a sequencing check are valuable alternatives serving different purposes.
misconceptions: Thinking all stars end the same way — not realising a star's MASS decides whether it becomes a white dwarf or explodes as a supernova.
Believing stars are 'on fire'/burning like a bonfire, rather than shining by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium.
Thinking we can watch a single star go through its life — missing that the stages take millions/billions of years and we infer the cycle from many stars at different stages.
Assuming bigger stars live longer (they actually burn out far faster) — confusing size with lifespan.
Thinking a star's death is a total disappearance, not realising it leaves a remnant (white dwarf, or after a supernova a dense core) and scatters material that seeds new stars.
Confusing a nebula (gas-and-dust cloud where stars form) with a galaxy (a vast collection of stars).

activities.title: Set the mass, watch the fate
steps: Start with a glowing cloud of gas and dust (a nebula) on screen and a single MASS dial/slider as the control.

Set the mass LOW and press play: watch the cloud collapse, a star ignite (hydrogen fusing into helium), shine steadily for a very long time, then swell into a giant and gently puff off a glowing ring, leaving a tiny white ember (white dwarf).
Rewind, crank the mass dial HIGH, and press play again: watch the star blaze through its life startlingly fast, swell into a supergiant, and end in a blinding supernova.
Read a lifespan counter each run so the 'live fast, die young' contrast is concrete — the massive star's counter runs out far sooner.
Try a 'Sun' preset that drops a marker on the main sequence 'here, now', roughly halfway along the gentle low-mass path.
Say in your own words what stayed the same across both runs and what changed.
activities.insight: It is the SAME kind of birth for every star; how massive the star is decides how it dies — and the biggest stars die youngest, not oldest.

activities.title: Walk the branching life-cycle diagram
steps: Follow a labelled life-cycle flow with the fork at the main-sequence stage: nebula → main-sequence star, then branching to [low mass → giant → white dwarf] OR [high mass → supergiant → supernova].
Tap each stage to reveal what is happening there (gravity clumps gas; the core fuses hydrogen into helium; the star swells; the ending).
Use the clearly labelled fork marked 'small star' vs 'massive star' to state which ending each path leads to and why.
Open the flap on the Sun to read 'a main-sequence star, about halfway through its life'.
Retell the whole sequence from memory, naming each stage including the giant or supergiant step.
activities.insight: The life cycle has a clear, retellable shape with named stages, and the ending forks on whether the star is small (giant → white dwarf) or massive (supergiant → supernova).

activities.title: Awe imagery of birth and death
steps: View real imagery of a star nursery nebula (e.g. the Orion Nebula), the Sun as an ordinary main-sequence star, and a supernova remnant.
Optionally take a fly-through of a nebula or a supernova set-piece as a wonder moment.
Match each image to its place on the life-cycle story you learned.
Discuss why we never watch one star change: stages take millions to billions of years, so we see many stars at different stages — like photographing a forest to infer one tree's life.
activities.insight: The abstract timescales become tangible and awe-inspiring through real images, and we infer the cycle from many stars caught at different stages rather than watching one.

activities.title: Check the sequence and the branch
steps: Put the life stages in order with the branch intact: nebula → main-sequence star → then either (low mass) giant → white dwarf, or (high mass) supergiant → supernova.
Answer: 'What single property decides whether a star becomes a white dwarf or a supernova?' (its mass).
Match each mass (small / massive) to its ending (white dwarf / supernova).
Answer the surprise puzzle: which lasts longer, a huge massive star or a small one like the Sun — and why?
activities.insight: Learners can recall and apply the stage order and its branch, name mass as the deciding property, and recognise that massive stars live shortest.

checkQuestion: Our Sun is a fairly small-to-medium star. When it reaches the end of its life, will it explode in a giant supernova like the biggest stars do? And here's a puzzle: do the biggest, most massive stars live the LONGEST, because they have the most fuel? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: No — the Sun is too small to explode as a supernova. At the end of its life it will swell into a red giant, then gently shed its outer layers and shrink into a white dwarf; only much more massive stars end in supernovae. And the puzzle's answer is surprising: the biggest, most massive stars actually live the SHORTEST lives, not the longest. Even though they hold more fuel, they burn it enormously faster and more furiously, so they last only a few million years, while a small star like the Sun sips its fuel and shines for billions of years. A star's MASS decides both how it lives and how it dies.
